comments.story_title: Ask HN: Why Is Everything Declining?
comments.why_zh: 令人安心的视角：人类进步在背景中缓慢持续
comments.quote_zh: 每当我感觉和楼主类似时，我就会看 Hans Rosling [1] 的东西
comments.text_zh: 这只是个人经验，但每当我感觉和楼主类似时，我就会看 Hans Rosling [1] 或 Anna Rosling [2] 的东西。虽然它们分别有10年和5年了，但我觉得总体情绪仍然成立——人类进步是缓慢的，发生在背景中，在你特定的子群体里可能还在起起伏伏。而与当下、由媒体叙事驱动的当下相比，很难看到全球人口中正在发生的改善。这帮助我理清头绪——当然，效果因人而异（也许这只是帮我自欺欺人地走出低谷，但它确实管用！）。[1] Hans Rosling 的《200 Countries, 200 Years, 4 Minutes》——[VIDEO] [2] 看看世界其他地方的人如何生活，按收入排列——Anna Rosling Rönnlund [LINK]
comments.text: This is just personal but anytime I feel similar to the OP, I watch something by Hans Rosling [1] or Anna Rosling [2]. Although 10 and 5 years old respectively, I feel the general sentiment is still true - that human progress is slow, in the background and might be ebbing and flowing in your specific sub-population. And when compared to the present, media narrative driven present its hard to see the improvements happening across the global population. It helps me put stuff in perspective - of course mileage may var (and maybe it's just helping me delude myself into getting out a funk but it works!). [1] Hans Rosling's 200 Countries, 200 Years, 4 Minutes - [VIDEO] [2] See how the rest of the world lives, organized by income - Anna Rosling Rönnlund [LINK]

comments.quote_zh: 为了有个直观感受，花5分钟看看
comments.text_zh: 我是在就导致当前政策的推理过程发表看法。我不是说这些政策执行得好（其实我认为并不好），我只是说，它们除了“奖励关系硬的游说团体”之外，还有别的理由来为自身辩护。至于非洲的贫困和饥荒，你说得对，富裕国家保护农民的措施会伤害贫穷国家的农民。然而，非洲饥荒的头号原因仍然是非洲内部的腐败和战争。而且按照当前的经济趋势，未来几十年我们会看到非洲出现经济强国。所以，尽管我们对十多亿非洲人利益的忽视令人悲哀，但这似乎并不是永久踩在别人脸上的一脚。为了有个直观感受，花5分钟看看[VIDEO]。就在今天，有些非洲国家的状况比70年前世界上任何国家都更好。如果其他国家沿着别处已经发生的趋势继续走下去，情况会相当显著地改善。我同意你，我们的农业政策造成了问题。但我对受影响的人们的未来感到乐观。
comments.text: I am making a statement about the reasoning that results in current policies. I'm not saying that the policies are well-executed (indeed I think they are not), merely that they have something more than just "reward a well-connected lobby" justifying them. As for African poverty and famine, you're right that measures that protect farmers in rich countries will hurt farmers in poor ones. However the #1 cause of African famine remains corruption and war inside of Africa. And on current economic trends, we'll see economic powerhouses emerging in Africa in near decades. So as sad as our neglect of the interests of over a billion Africans is, it does not seem to be a permanent boot in the face. For perspective, take 5 minutes to watch [VIDEO] . There are - today - African countries that are better off than any country in the world was 70 years ago. If others continue on trends that have happened elsewhere, things are going to improve fairly dramatically. I agree with you that our agricultural policies create problems. But I'm optimistic about what the future holds for people who are impacted.

comments.text: Not utopia compared to what? My great grandmother had to have 8 kids so that she could have 4 or 5 adult children. That was less than 100 years ago. My grand parents were the children of subsistence farmers without running water or electricity. They went to high school, worked in factories, and could get broadcast TV in their living room. Electricity and running water became a base default. My parents work in an office pushing papers around. Even the society of their youth seems alien in its antiquatedness of both social mores and amenities. I get paid to think things and can reasonably expect to live essentially disease free until my 70's. Achieving 90 in relatively good health and vitality doesn't seem out of the question. Seems pretty utopic to me. What not-utopia are you talking about? EDIT: Watch: [VIDEO] Over the past 200 years, the difference between 1st world and 3rd world has all but vanished. We still have a ways to go, but no utopia is perfect. Even in the movies.

comments.text: Fair point. In defense of my moral model, it's backed up by this idea: are things perfect? No. Is the system working? Yes, and astonishingly well. Is there a better way to get from here to there, where "there" is some improved state of prosperity and development? No. Human nature is what it is, and our systems must exploit our nature rather than combat it. It's all based on measurable positive outcomes, rather than some theoretical idea that being eye-wateringly rich is somehow bad - morally bad, or bad for society. That idea is rooted in the old, pre-growth, pre-industrial paradigm, when all wealth was seized by force in some way. Today, some wealth is from violence, but the overwhelming majority is new money that was created out of nothing but good old human intelligence. comments.text_zh: 我认为一个社区拥有本地道路、也就是最后一英里，是合理的。但我不认为高速公路由政府控制合理，除非那里没有竞争。去大多数地方都有很多条路可走。即便是垄断，也存在一个让道路赚最多钱的价格水平。超过那个水平，你就无法再提价而不亏钱。即便如此，社区也可以与道路提供方签合同，按每英里付钱给提供方，但把动态定价的收益归社区。而且当然，社区必须同意接入并使用某条道路，它才能盈利。我们当然不希望出现像那条连接美国和加拿大的私人所有桥梁那样的情况——附近没有别的桥。但我开车去皇后区付的过桥费还更高。我完全支持把收益最大化。正因为如此，我们才应该为使用道路付费，尤其是在高峰时段。因为道路免费的时候，我们在上面浪费了大量时间。这不是为了给政府收最多的钱，而是在需求最高的时候让交通流量最大化。没错，在没有强市场和产权的地方，吃饭很难。过去30年情况大大改善了，人们现在拥有更多权利，食品价格由市场决定，而不是由政治决策决定。[视频] 价格越准确，我们的决策就越合理，机会也越多
comments.text: I think it makes sense for a community to own its local roads, the last mile. But I don't think government control makes sense for highways, except perhaps where there is no competition. There are many ways to get to most places. Even with a monopoly, there is a price level where the road makes the most money. You can't raise prices above that without losing money. Even then, it is possible for communities to have contracts with road providers that pay a provider for each mile travelled but that give the community the proceeds of the surge pricing. And certainly communities have to agree to connect to and use a road for it to be profitable. And we certainly don't want to have a situation like that privately owned bridge connecting the US and Canada where there are no other bridges nearby. But I pay an even higher bridge toll to drive to Queens. I'm all for maximizing the benefits. That is the reason we should have to pay to use roads, especially at peak times. Because we waste a lot of time on them when they are free. It's not about collecting the most money for the government. It's about maximizing the flow of traffic when demand is highest. And yes, its hard to eat in places without strong markets and property rights. And things have improved greatly over the last 30 years where people now have more rights and markets set the prices for food rather than political decisions. comments.text_zh: > 三百年前，全职妻子每周要做大约60小时的家务。在省力机器出现之前，这还是个严重低估的数字。这里有一个关于“3500美元的衬衫”的演讲，以及女性在任何空闲时间都在纺线的事实：[LINK] 这是 Hans Rosling 关于财富的可视化：[VIDEO] 我记得一个关于一对历史学家夫妇的故事（可惜找不到出处了），他们试图按1880年代的方式生活。丈夫基本上每天回到家都筋疲力尽。而妻子则真的崩溃了，因为家务完全没完没了。她每一个醒着的时刻都在忙着维持这个家。大家庭的存在不仅仅是因为缺乏节育手段。
comments.text: > Three hundred years ago, full-time wives did about 60 hours/week of housework. This is a woeful underestimate before labor saving machinery. Here is a talk about the $3500 Shirt and the fact that women spun thread in any idle time: [LINK] Here is a Hans Rosling visualization of wealth: [VIDEO] I remember a story about historian couple (sadly I can't find it) who tried to live like the 1880's. The husband basically came home completely exhausted every single day. The wife, however, literally broke down because the housework was completely relentless. She was completely busy maintaining the household every single waking moment. Big families weren't just because of lack of birth control.

comments.text_zh: 我很无聊，所以回一下。不过从哪儿说起呢？首先，货币最基本的作用是作为交易媒介。在合理开销和可接受时间内，人们需要能用钱换到商品和服务。加密货币在每一个实际层面都做不到。如果我想用 bitcoin 买披萨，我的开销会超过披萨本身的价值，完成购买的平均时间比下单、做好、送达并被我的家人吃掉的平均时间还长。（你见过饥饿的青少年扑向披萨的样子吗？）而且，如果人们开始尝试用 bitcoin 买披萨，你很快会遇到一个问题：bitcoin 网络每秒最大交易数只是每秒售出披萨数量的一小部分。是是是，这些都可以改进。这话我听了多年。但这些问题并不新，也没有消失。好，接下来呢？你把一个事实大做文章：在一些糟糕的第三世界国家，有穷人想用加密货币逃避威权监管。往好了说，这是转移注意力；我更倾向于说它不诚实。加密货币一个重要得多的用例，是犯罪分子试图在不被执法部门抓住的情况下，为他们的勒索软件攻击获得报酬。而第三世界从 M-PESA 这类支付网络获得的好处，远远超过所有加密货币带来的好处。此外，帮助糟糕第三世界国家穷人的最好办法，就是继续推动全球经济发展……
comments.text: I'm bored, so I'll respond. But where to begin? First, the most basic role of money is to be a medium of exchange. With reasonable overhead and in acceptable time, people need to be able to exchange money for goods and services. Crypto fails this in every practical way. If I want to buy pizza with bitcoin, my overhead exceeds the value of the pizza, the average time to make the purchase is longer than the average time to order, have it made, delivered, and get eaten by my family. (Have you ever SEEN hungry teenagers tear into pizza.) Also if people started trying to buy pizza with bitcoin, you'd quickly run into the problem that the maximum number of transactions per second on the bitcoin network is a fraction of the number of pizzas sold per second. Yes, yes. This is all improvable. I've heard that for years. But these issues are not new, and haven't gone away. OK, what next? You are making a big deal out of the fact that there are poor people in horrible third world countries who want to use crypto to escape authoritarian oversight. At best this is a red herring, I lean towards calling it disingenuous. A far more important use case for crypto is crooks trying to get paid for their ransomware attacks without themselves being caught by law enforcement. And the third world has benefitted far more from payment networks like M-PESA than all of crypto.
